title: One ummah, many faces
hook: Arab, Persian, Turkish, African, Malay, Chinese, European

segments.voice: Yesterday: unsung women, Zubayda's wells, Fatima in Fez, Karima teaching in Mecca, Nana Asma'u in Sokoto. Your line was they were there.

Friday, in a big-city mosque. The row forms, shoulder to shoulder. On the left, a taxi driver whose family came from Cairo. Next to him a student from Istanbul, then a grandfather from Lagos, a nurse whose parents came from Kuala Lumpur, a man from Xi'an in a white cap, a convert from Sarajevo, an engineer from Tehran. Different languages in the parking lot, different food at home, different ways of tying a headscarf or a turban. Then the imam says God is greatest, and every one of them raises their hands at once. Today: one ummah, many faces.
screen: `ONE ROW, SHOULDER TO SHOULDER.` → `CAIRO, ISTANBUL, LAGOS, KUALA LUMPUR.` → `ONE MOVEMENT.`

segments.voice: Ummah is the Arabic word for a community, a people, and Muslims use it for the whole worldwide community of believers. First, the Qur'an names it as one. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! this, your religion, is one religion, and I am your Lord, so worship Me." Second, the many faces were there among the Prophet's own companions. Bilal, of Abyssinian descent, gave his voice to the call to prayer. Salman came from Persia, searching for the truth. Suhayb, who grew up among the Byzantines, was called the Roman. The community around the Prophet, peace be upon him, was mixed before it was large. Third, the line that set the rule. In the sermon of the Prophet's last pilgrimage, as Musnad Ahmad reports it, he said no Arab is above a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab above an Arab, nor a light-skinned person above a dark-skinned one, nor the other way, except by piety. Rank by birth was cut off at the root. Fourth, what the history adds. This path has walked through Arab caliphs, Persian poets, Turkish sultans, West African scholars, Malay sultanates, Chinese mosques and the old Muslims of the Balkans. They prayed toward the same house in Mecca, in Arabic, then went home and cooked their own food, sang their own songs and built in their own style. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari pictures believers as one body: when one part aches, the whole body feels it. One body, many faces. The history suggests that's a feature, not a problem to fix.
screen: `ONE RELIGION, ONE LORD.` · `BILAL, SALMAN, SUHAYB: A MIXED CIRCLE.` · `NO ARAB ABOVE A NON-ARAB, EXCEPT BY PIETY.` · `ONE BODY, MANY FACES.`

segments.voice: Choose the place from today you know least about, West Africa, Malaysia, China, Bosnia, Iran, Turkey, Egypt, and picture someone there right now at the same prayer, saying the same Arabic words in a room that looks nothing like yours. What are they wearing, what does the street sound like, what will they eat after? If you pray, remember them in your next prayer.
One ummah. The worldwide community of Muslims: one religion, one direction of prayer, and every face, language and culture inside it. Today's word.
Your line: many faces. One body, and every part feels the others. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims of every background pray in the same rows, facing the Ka'ba in Mecca and reciting in Arabic, while keeping their own languages, dress, food and festivals.

chat.says: If Muslims come from so many cultures, what makes them one community?
options: One religion, one Lord, one qibla; nobody ranks above another by birth.
They all share Arab descent, going back to the Prophet's family.
They must all adopt the same food, dress and customs as Mecca.

Editor: Bilal was born in Mecca of Abyssinian descent, so 'came from Abyssinia' became 'of Abyssinian descent'; Salman joined in Medina, so 'the first circle' / 'first companions' became 'the Prophet's own companions'; the farewell-sermon line now runs both ways, as the hadith does.

Audit: Suhayb al-Rumi was, by the standard accounts, of Arab descent (Namir), taken captive as a child and raised among the Byzantines, hence 'the Roman'. The teach and the myth reveal had offered him as evidence that the companions were not all Arabs; both now say he 'grew up among the Byzantines', and the myth's non-Arab evidence rests on Bilal and Salman.
